content: System monitoring, research, and innovation are critical components of advancing oral health. This includes establishing a national oral health research priority agenda and ensuring the effective translation of evidence and data into actionable strategies. Partnerships and engagement with civil society are essential to foster ownership, alignment, and acceleration of efforts in this domain. Appendix 4 provides a schematic overview of the fundamental operational and logistical functions of an oral health unit within a Ministry of Health. Such a unit should ideally be integrated or aligned with departments responsible for non-communicable diseases (NCDs), family health, life-course approaches, or other related areas. It should be guided by a national oral health policy, staffed with professionals possessing public health and administrative expertise, and included in the ministry’s overall budgeting process. The roles and responsibilities of key stakeholders in promoting oral health are extensive. These include national governments, subnational administrations, health regulatory bodies, professional associations, educational and research institutions, civil society organizations, the media, development partners, and individuals, families, and communities. Each stakeholder has a unique role in leading, managing, supporting, financing, advocating, and communicating efforts to improve oral health outcomes. For example, national governments are tasked with strengthening advocacy and political commitment for oral health, adapting the South-East Asia Oral Health Action Plan (2022–2030) to their national context, and developing policies, legislation, and standards to integrate oral health into NCDs, primary health care (PHC), and universal health coverage (UHC). They must also allocate appropriate resources, coordinate with other ministries, and promote workforce planning, training, and retention of oral health professionals. Subnational administrations are responsible for prioritizing oral health in planning and implementation frameworks, providing technical support, and engaging communities in improving their oral and general health. Professional associations facilitate continuous professional development, maintain ethical standards, and advocate for oral health at all levels. Educational and research institutions play a pivotal role in developing training curricula aligned with national needs and international standards, conducting research to inform policy, and recommending evidence-based approaches for oral disease management. The media supports advocacy and raises awareness about oral health issues, while development partners integrate oral health into broader NCD interventions, provide technical support, and mobilize resources. Communities, families, and individuals are encouraged to participate in local priority setting, advocate for community-based oral health programs, and support the implementation of policies such as smoke-free environments and improved hygiene practices. They are also urged to act as role models for promoting oral health. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides leadership and coordination to promote and monitor the implementation of the South-East Asia Oral Health Action Plan (2022–2030). WHO offers technical support, collaborates with United Nations agencies and other partners, and develops guidance documents to align national efforts with global policies, such as the Global Oral Health Action Plan (2023–2030). Monitoring and reporting on the progress of the action plan are essential for transparency, informed decision-making, and stakeholder engagement. WHO’s global strategy on oral health emphasizes improving surveillance, data collection, and monitoring to guide advocacy and policy decisions. This includes standardizing methods for gathering epidemiological data, integrating electronic dental and medical records, and strengthening surveillance of oral diseases. Operational research and evaluation of interventions are also critical components. Tracking progress toward 2030 goals for both the global and regional oral health strategies is vital. The global monitoring framework, which includes indicators and reporting mechanisms, is evolving, and the regional framework will be updated to align closely with global policies, reducing the reporting burden on countries. Strengthening information systems and improving data availability are key actions proposed in this document. Specific targets include a 3% reduction in premature mortality from oral cancer by 2030 and a 25% reduction in the prevalence of untreated dental caries in permanent teeth. These targets rely on robust data collection systems, such as death registration systems and population-based surveys, to monitor progress effectively. Promotive, preventive, curative, and rehabilitative oral health services are outlined to address common population needs. These include counseling on oral hygiene, nutrition, and tobacco cessation; screening for oral diseases, cancer, and developmental anomalies; emergency management of oral conditions; and comprehensive treatment options such as fluoride varnish application, restorative treatments, and management of oral cancer and HIV-related manifestations. A functioning oral health unit within a Ministry of Health should be fully integrated with related health programs and guided by evidence-informed policies. Adaptations to organizational models should align with national priorities and principles. In summary, the collective efforts of governments, stakeholders, and communities are essential to achieving the goals of the South-East Asia Oral Health Action Plan and ensuring universal access to oral health care by 2030.
